title: Multisig classification is re-verified quarterly and after material change, because declared purpose drifts from actual use
content:
A.2.11.1.3.3.1 requires Core GovOps to engage the Protocol Security Workstream Lead "and third party providers" for periodic reviews confirming that "documentation, configuration, and operational classification remain accurate and aligned with current usage," on three triggers: quarterly as a minimum, "following major operational, financial, or structural changes," and "when significant protocol changes materially affect the Multisig's role, authority, or risk exposure."

The review scope (A.2.11.1.3.3.1.1) names what actually goes stale: registry accuracy, "[r]eassessment of Multisig operational purpose where operational patterns change," and "[r]eassessment of financial exposure or protocol impact where asset exposure or operational scope changes."

This closes the framework's largest gap. Classification is self-assessed once at setup and determines every downstream requirement — threshold, signer count, drills, availability. But a multisig set up for a modest purpose accumulates responsibilities and balances, and nothing in the setup rules notices. A multisig classified Medium at 900,000 USD that now holds several million is non-compliant with the seven-signer rule without anyone having done anything wrong.

Bringing in third-party providers is the other notable choice: it puts eyes on the configuration that are not the administrator who chose it and not the Lead who approved it.

Crucially, review has consequences rather than producing a report — A.2.11.1.3.3.2 routes any identified inconsistency, outdated documentation, or potential noncompliance directly into the enforcement provision.
description: Core GovOps, the Protocol Security Workstream Lead and third-party providers reassess documentation, purpose, exposure and configuration against how the multisig is actually being used.
